E1: GitHub, Application card: GitHub Copilot inline suggestions.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/github/docs/d0c59c59fadf92c3a44676a3ed7ed38a015379ca/content/copilot/responsible-use/inline-suggestions.md
Section 1, exact excerpt: "GitHub Copilot inline suggestions provide autocomplete-style suggestions as you work. These suggestions appear inline in your editor or in text fields on GitHub.com, helping you write code and pull request descriptions more quickly."
Section 4, exact excerpt: "Copilot can suggest test cases based on the surrounding code, including possible input parameters, expected output values, and assertions. This helps developers create test coverage more quickly, including edge cases and boundary conditions that might be difficult to identify manually. Generated tests should still be reviewed, as they may not cover all scenarios."
Section 6, exact excerpt: "The surrounding code from your cursor position is pre-processed by the inline suggestions system, combined with contextual information (such as code snippets from open tabs in the editor), and sent to a large language model in the form of a prompt."
Section 7, exact excerpt: "Copilot may generate code that appears to be valid but may not actually be semantically or syntactically correct or may not accurately reflect the intent of the developer."
Interpretation limits: vendor statements of intended capability and risk, not measured net productivity, reliability, confidentiality guarantees, or proof of local suitability. Context processing makes permitted data exposure a decision question. Do not infer a specific retention, training-use, hosting or licensing term from these passages.

organization: SYNTHETIC CASE P: mid-sized business-software company; 80 developers, of whom 12 could join a limited initiative. No actual company is represented.
industry_sector: B2B workflow software for commercial clients; routine maintenance can affect customers but this case excludes safety-critical and payment authorization logic.
users_stakeholders: Developers, two available senior reviewers, engineering manager, security lead, customer-support staff and business customers.
adoption_posture: Moderate / fast follower. Management will fund evidence gathering but wants demonstrated local benefit before routine use.
capabilities_constraints: Scenario assumptions: Existing pull-request review, CI unit/integration tests and static security scans are enforced. Two senior reviewers can each allocate four hours per week for six weeks; this is a capacity cap, not proof that it is sufficient. A security lead can authorize a restricted workspace containing only internally owned low-sensitivity modules and synthetic fixtures. Third-party licensed modules, secrets and customer records must remain excluded; full-service contractual review for proprietary code is not completed. Up to 12 seats and 60 staff-hours of incremental evaluation/review time are available across six weeks; subscription cost is unquoted and this is not an approved purchase. Historical conventional-workflow timestamps and defect tickets exist but task matching and review-time measurement have not been designed. No controlled local AI result exists.
risk_consequence_context: Scenario assumptions: A bad change can interrupt customer workflows and require support/rework. Isolated branches and test fixtures allow pre-release rejection; a feature flag and deployment rollback are available, with a target operational recovery time of one business day, not a guarantee. Leaked customer data cannot be recalled, so that exposure is excluded rather than considered reversible. A normal release still needs release-manager approval. Review and CI reduce exposure but do not prove correctness or eliminate tail risks.
